questions.text: A tower controller issues: 'Cessna 3AB, hold short of Runway 24L.' The pilot reads back: 'Roger, Cessna 3AB.' Is this readback adequate?

options.label: A
options.text: No. The pilot must read back the full hold-short instruction including the runway identifier: 'Hold short of Runway 24L, Cessna 3AB.' 'Roger' only means 'I received your transmission' — it does NOT constitute acknowledgment of a hold-short instruction. Without a complete readback, the controller cannot verify the pilot understood which runway to hold short of, creating a high risk of runway incursion.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes. 'Roger' means the pilot received and understood the instruction. A full readback is only required for IFR clearances, not VFR hold-short instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes. The pilot included their callsign in the readback, which satisfies the readback requirement. The specific hold-short instruction is implied.

options.label: D
options.text: No, but only because the pilot should have said 'Wilco' instead of 'Roger.' 'Wilco' indicates the pilot will comply with the hold-short instruction.

questions.explanation: Hold-short instructions require a FULL readback including the runway identifier. 'Roger' means only 'I received your transmission' — it does not indicate compliance or understanding. The closed-loop readback is the primary defense against expectation bias and runway incursions. Option D is partially correct that 'Wilco' implies compliance, but even 'Wilco' alone without the runway identifier is insufficient — the full instruction must be repeated to close the communication loop.

questions.text: A pilot is diverting to an unfamiliar airport due to deteriorating weather. The VFR Sectional chart shows a frequency box but the text is partially obscured by an airspace boundary line. What is the fastest reliable method to obtain the correct CTAF frequency in flight?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the GPS or EFB 'Nearest Airport' function to look up the airport. Modern avionics databases and EFB apps display CTAF, tower, and AWOS frequencies for nearby airports. Cross-reference with the Chart Supplement if time permits, but the database lookup is the fastest in-flight method during an active diversion.

options.label: B
options.text: Try 122.8 MHz — it is the universal CTAF used at all non-towered airports in the United States. If no response, try 121.5 MHz.

options.label: C
options.text: Contact Flight Service on 122.2 MHz and ask them to look up the frequency. Flight Service has access to all airport data and can relay the CTAF.

options.label: D
options.text: Attempt to read the partially obscured frequency box more carefully. The sectional chart is the most reliable source and should always be used over electronic databases.

questions.explanation: During an active diversion with time pressure, the GPS/EFB 'Nearest' function provides the fastest frequency lookup. It displays all relevant frequencies (CTAF, Tower, AWOS) in seconds. Option B is dangerous — 122.8 is common but NOT universal. Many airports use different frequencies, and assuming 122.8 could result in transmitting on a dead channel while traffic operates on the actual CTAF. Option C is valid but slower — Flight Service can help, but the GPS lookup is immediate. Option D wastes time trying to read an obscured chart when faster electronic sources are available.

questions.text: During cruise flight in Class E airspace, a pilot's COM 1 radio stops transmitting — the pilot can hear ATC but cannot respond. COM 2 appears dead as well. Before declaring a radio failure, what troubleshooting steps should the pilot take?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the audio panel MIC selector — it may be set to COM 2 while the frequency is on COM 1 (or vice versa), causing transmissions on the wrong radio. Check headset jack for partial disconnection. Verify volume and squelch settings on both COMs. Check circuit breakers for the COM radios and audio panel. Try the handheld backup radio if available. If COM 2 appears dead, the audio panel speaker/receiver button for COM 2 may be deselected — the radio may be functioning but the pilot cannot hear it.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately squawk 7700 and begin descending toward the nearest airport. A dual radio failure indicates a serious electrical system malfunction that may affect other critical systems.

options.label: C
options.text: Cycle the avionics master switch off and on to reset both radios. If they don't come back, pull and reset the main avionics circuit breaker.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the flight in silence — as long as the pilot maintains VFR and stays out of controlled airspace, radio communication is not legally required in Class E airspace.

questions.explanation: The majority of 'radio failures' are caused by simple configuration errors, not equipment failures. The audio panel is the most common culprit — the MIC selector determines which COM the pilot transmits on, and the speaker/receiver buttons determine which COM the pilot hears. A MIC selector mismatch means the pilot is transmitting on a radio they can't hear responses from. Headset jack issues are the second most common cause. Option B is premature — 7700 is for emergencies, not radio troubleshooting. 7600 is the correct code for confirmed lost comm. Option C risks losing all avionics settings and may not address the root cause. Option D ignores the requirement for two-way communication when receiving ATC services.

questions.text: A pilot has confirmed a complete radio failure (both COMs inoperative) while VFR in Class E airspace, 30 miles from the destination Class D airport. What is the correct sequence of actions?

options.label: A
options.text: Squawk 7600 on the transponder. Continue the flight under VFR toward the destination airport. Remain at or above the traffic pattern altitude to observe the active runway and traffic flow. Sequence into the traffic pattern visually. Look toward the control tower for light gun signals — a steady green light means cleared to land. Acknowledge by rocking wings (day) or flashing lights (night). Land as soon as practicable.

options.label: B
options.text: Squawk 7700 on the transponder. Divert immediately to the nearest non-towered airport to avoid Class D airspace. A NORDO aircraft cannot legally enter Class D airspace under any circumstances.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue to the Class D airport but remain outside the airspace boundary and circle until ATC sends a helicopter to escort the aircraft into the pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Land at the nearest available field or road — a dual radio failure is an emergency that requires an immediate off-airport landing to preserve safety.

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.185(b) governs this situation: in VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable. 7600 is the correct squawk for lost communications (not 7700, which is for emergencies). The Class D tower has light gun procedures specifically designed for NORDO aircraft — this is why light guns exist. The pilot can enter Class D airspace; the tower will use light signals to manage the aircraft. Option B incorrectly uses 7700 and states NORDO aircraft cannot enter Class D — this is false. The light gun system enables exactly this scenario. Option D treats lost comm as an emergency requiring off-airport landing — it is not.

questions.text: What is the precise distinction between 'Roger' and 'Wilco' in aviation radio communication?

options.label: A
options.text: 'Roger' means 'I have received ALL of your last transmission.' It confirms receipt only — it does NOT imply the pilot will comply. 'Wilco' means 'I have received your message and WILL COMPLY with it.' 'Wilco' inherently includes 'Roger' — saying 'Roger Wilco' is redundant. Using 'Roger' in response to an instruction that requires action (like a frequency change) is ambiguous because it does not confirm compliance.

options.label: B
options.text: 'Roger' and 'Wilco' are interchangeable terms both meaning 'I understand and will comply.' The choice between them is a matter of personal preference.

options.label: C
options.text: 'Roger' is used for VFR communications and 'Wilco' is used for IFR communications. They have the same meaning but are designated for different types of flight operations.

options.label: D
options.text: 'Roger' means 'I agree with your instruction' and 'Wilco' means 'I will comply as soon as possible.' The distinction is about timing — 'Wilco' implies delayed compliance.

questions.explanation: Per the Pilot/Controller Glossary: 'Roger' = 'I have received all of your last transmission.' It is an acknowledgment of receipt, NOT a commitment to action. 'Wilco' = 'I have received your message and will comply.' It includes receipt AND commitment. Because 'Wilco' already includes the meaning of 'Roger,' saying 'Roger Wilco' is redundant (though common). The distinction matters: if ATC says 'Change to frequency 124.6' and the pilot responds 'Roger,' the controller does not know if the pilot will actually switch. 'Wilco' confirms the switch will happen.

questions.text: During departure from a towered airport, a pilot is instructed: 'Contact Departure on 124.6.' The pilot loads 124.6 into the COM 1 standby, presses the transfer button, and transmits: 'Departure, Cessna 3AB, passing through two thousand.' There is no response. After two more attempts with no response, what is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The audio panel MIC selector is likely still set to COM 2 from an earlier configuration. The pilot pressed the transfer button on COM 1, correctly loading 124.6 into the active slot. However, if the MIC selector is on COM 2, the pilot's transmissions are going out on whatever frequency is tuned on COM 2 — not on 124.6. The fix: verify the MIC selector switch matches COM 1.

options.label: B
options.text: The departure frequency is incorrect — 124.6 may have changed since the last chart update. The pilot should return to the tower frequency and request the current departure frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: Departure control's radar may not have acquired the aircraft yet. The pilot should continue climbing and try again at a higher altitude when radar line-of-sight is better.

options.label: D
options.text: The COM 1 radio has failed. The pilot should switch to COM 2, tune 124.6, and try again.

questions.explanation: The audio panel MIC selector mismatch is the most common cause of 'no response' after a frequency change. The pilot correctly tuned COM 1 but may be transmitting on COM 2 (which has a different frequency loaded). The fix is simple: check the MIC selector switch. This is a configuration error, not an equipment failure. Option B is possible but unlikely — frequencies don't change without NOTAM publication. Option C is possible at very low altitudes but unlikely during a normal departure. Option D assumes hardware failure when the most common cause is a software/configuration issue.

questions.text: A pilot is taxiing at an unfamiliar Class C airport. The ground controller issues a lengthy taxi clearance: 'Taxi to Runway 22L via Bravo, Charlie, cross Runway 36, hold short of Taxiway Delta.' The pilot is only 60% sure they heard it correctly. What should the pilot do?

options.label: A
options.text: Read back what the pilot thinks they heard and begin taxiing. If the readback is wrong, the controller will correct it.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop the aircraft. Request 'Say again' from the controller. Write the clearance on the kneeboard as the controller repeats it. Read back the complete clearance including the hold-short instruction and runway crossing. Do not move until the readback is confirmed correct. Then pull up the airport diagram and trace the route before releasing the brakes.

options.label: C
options.text: Begin taxiing slowly and follow the blue taxiway lights toward Runway 22L. The general direction is clear even if the specific route is uncertain. If the pilot ends up on the wrong taxiway, the controller will see it on surface radar and correct them.

options.label: D
options.text: Read back only the hold-short instruction ('Hold short of Delta') and begin taxiing, figuring out the route as they go. The hold-short is the safety-critical element; the taxi route is less important.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A (impulsivity) guesses and moves — a wrong readback may be corrected, but a wrong TURN may not be caught before it becomes an incursion. Option C (invulnerability) relies on ATC as a safety net — controllers can miss surface movements, especially at night or during high traffic. Option D partially complies but ignores the runway crossing ('cross Runway 36'), which is equally safety-critical. Option B uses all available tools: stopping to build SA, requesting a repeat, writing it down, full readback with confirmation, and route tracing before moving.
questions.explanation: Uncertain taxi clearances at unfamiliar airports are a primary cause of runway incursions. There is ZERO stigma in requesting 'Say again' — controllers expect it, especially from unfamiliar pilots at complex airports. The write-read-trace sequence (write the clearance, read it back, trace it on the diagram) is the standard of care for complex taxi operations.

questions.text: During a night cross-country, an aircraft's engine begins running rough and losing RPM. Carburetor heat does not resolve the issue. The aircraft is slowly losing altitude. The pilot has been troubleshooting silently for 3 minutes without contacting ATC. What should the pilot do?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue troubleshooting in silence — the pilot should resolve the engine issue before adding the distraction of radio communication. ATC will only complicate the situation with unnecessary questions.

options.label: B
options.text: Declare an emergency immediately: 'Center, Cessna 123AB, declaring an emergency, partial engine failure, losing altitude, turning direct nearest airport.' Squawk 7700. An emergency declaration gives the pilot legal authority to deviate from any rule, triggers priority handling, and activates crash-fire-rescue alerting. The 3 minutes spent troubleshooting in silence wasted critical time during which ATC could have been clearing airspace, vectoring to the nearest airport, and alerting rescue services.

options.label: C
options.text: Wait until the engine either recovers or fails completely before declaring an emergency. Declaring an emergency for a rough-running engine is an overreaction that will generate unnecessary paperwork and FAA attention.

options.label: D
options.text: Transmit 'Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan' on the current frequency. This urgency call is more appropriate than a full emergency declaration for a partial power loss that has not yet resulted in complete engine failure.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A (anti-authority) treats ATC as a distraction — ATC is a massive resource that exists precisely for this situation. Option C (macho) waits for total failure — by then, the pilot may be too low to reach an airport. The 'paperwork myth' is false: 14 CFR 91.3(c) requires a written report ONLY if requested by the Administrator. Option D (resignation) uses Pan-Pan, which is technically appropriate for urgency, but the situation — rough engine, losing RPM, losing altitude at night — has already crossed into distress. A full emergency declaration is warranted. Option B correctly prioritizes immediate declaration, maximizing the time window for ATC to provide resources.
questions.explanation: Hesitation to declare an emergency is a documented killer in GA. 14 CFR 91.3(b) gives the PIC authority to deviate from ANY rule during an in-flight emergency. ATC immediately clears airspace, provides vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and alerts crash-fire-rescue. The only cost is a potential written report IF the FAA requests one — and even that is unlikely for a legitimate emergency. Three minutes of silent troubleshooting while losing altitude at night represents three minutes of wasted resources that could save the pilot's life.
